description: Rhenium is a silvery-gray, heavy, third-row transition metal in group 7 of the periodic table with atomic number 75. With an estimated average concentration of 1 part per billion, it is one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust. It has one of the highest melting and boiling points of any element and can assume oxidation states ranging from −3 to +7.
uses: Nickel-based superalloys of rhenium are used in combustion chambers, turbine blades, and exhaust nozzles of jet engines, making jet engine construction the largest single use for the element. The second-most important use is as a catalyst, where it is excellent for hydrogenation and isomerization, particularly in catalytic reforming of naphtha for use in gasoline through the rheniforming process. Platinum-rhenium catalysts are also primarily used in making lead-free, high-octane gasoline.
characteristics: Rhenium is a silvery-white metal with one of the highest melting points of all elements, exceeded only by tungsten, and has one of the highest boiling points among stable elements. It is also one of the densest elements, exceeded only by platinum, iridium, and osmium, with a hexagonal close-packed crystal structure. When annealed, it is very ductile and can be bent, coiled, or rolled, and it resists alkalis and common acids at room temperature and atmospheric pressure.
